title: PythonU (Python Unicode) - Separating programming keywords from everyday English
author: Abeggar
Nodd
text: There are some existing projects witch use a different approach for an equivalent result, see zhpy · PyPI in Chinese or frython · PyPI in French. I didn’t find anything in Vietnamese, but it could be adapted from these project.

author: Rosuav
text:
Alpha Beggar:

Since Python is a programming language, I think it should have its own separate set of characters for keywords (if, then, for, etc.) instead of sharing letters with normal English.





 Alpha Beggar:


Since code editors (Notepad++, VS Code) don’t support this yet, we can temporarily use tools like AutoHotkey to convert text into these Unicode points. For example, typing \if would automatically turn into the single [if] gray block.



So… you would still just type the keywords.
I recommend you look into some fonts with programming ligatures; they change the visual appearance of keywords and other symbols (like == or >=) without changing how you type in code, and without creating a different and incompatible Python.
If that’s not sufficient, build yourself a translator. Make a tool - in Python initially, but you can later “bootstrap” it by writing the tool in PythonU - that translates PythonU code into Python. (Also, I recommend coming up with a more different name; for now, include your own name or username in it, eg I might call mine “RosPython”.) Then build an editor that lets you input that any way you want.
But honestly, I’ve never found keywords like if and while to be the sticking point. If people don’t want to write code, it’s because of the entire concept of syntax, not because it uses familiar words. In fact, it’s much more likely that using familiar words is a benefit. Looking at your list of benefits:



 Alpha Beggar:

Doing this will make code much clearer, more accurate, faster to write, and faster to interpret.


Clearer? You propose a specialized font that then turns it back into the original word. More accurate? I’m not sure how much we gain by avoiding English letters in keywords, and what happens if one of these special characters comes up in a comment? It’s going to have to be interpreted exactly the same as its corresponding keyword anyway. Faster to write? No, because unless you design a keyboard with dedicated keys for these tokens, it’s going to be harder to write; and if you’re going to design a keyboard for yourself to use, it could just as easily put in the word if with a single button press. Faster to interpret? Python code gets parsed into an internal bytecode. The work of transforming human-readable text into bytecode is not a significant part of runtime for anything but the most trivial of scripts, so you aren’t going to gain anything meaningful.
Most of what you’re looking for can be achieved in better ways. There are already versions of Python with keywords translated into other languages; but if that’s not sufficient, consider the Scratch language and how it removes ALL syntax from programming. This is how you make something less daunting. Maybe what you could consider is making a Scratch-like interface that makes Python code as its back end. That would be far more effective IMO.

author: chepner
text: If you want to play with these ideas, try Haskell. It has very few keywords to start, lets you define your own operators, and supports Unicode.
